{{Short description|Mathematical model in fluid dynamics}}
[[Image:Mixing length.jpg|thumb|400px|The mixing length is a distance that a fluid [[fluid parcel|parcel]] will keep its original characteristics before dispersing them into the surrounding [[fluid mechanics|fluid]]. Here, the bar on the left side of the figure is the mixing length.]]

In [[fluid dynamics]],  the '''mixing length model''' is a method attempting to describe [[momentum]] transfer by [[turbulence]] [[Reynolds stresses]] within a [[Newtonian fluid]] [[boundary layer]] by means of an [[Viscosity#Eddy viscosity|eddy viscosity]]. The model was developed by [[Ludwig Prandtl]] in the early 20th century.<ref name="Holton">{{cite book |last=Holton |first=James R. |title=Dynamic Meteorology |edition=4th |series=International Geophysics Series |volume=88 |year=2004 |publisher=Elsevier Academic Press |location=Burlington, MA |pages=124–127 |chapter=Chapter 5 – The Planetary Boundary Layer }}</ref> Prandtl himself had reservations about the model,<ref name = "prandtl">{{cite journal | last = Prandtl | first = L. | title = 7. Bericht über Untersuchungen zur ausgebildeten Turbulenz | journal = Z. Angew. Math. Mech. | volume = 5 | issue = 1 | pages = 136–139 | date = 1925 | doi = 10.1002/zamm.19250050212 | bibcode = 1925ZaMM....5..136P | hdl = 2060/20050029454 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> describing it as, "only a rough approximation,"<ref name = "nature">{{cite journal | doi = 10.1038/249135b0 | last = Bradshaw | first = P. | title = Possible origin of Prandt's mixing-length theory  | journal = Nature | volume = 249 | issue = 6 | pages = 135–136 | date = 1974 | bibcode = 1974Natur.249..135B | s2cid = 4218601 }}</ref>
but it has been used in numerous fields ever since, including [[atmospheric science]], [[oceanography]] and [[stellar structure]].<ref name = "science">{{cite journal | doi = 10.1126/science.235.4787.465 | last = Chan | first = Kwing |author2=Sabatino Sofia | title = Validity Tests of the Mixing-Length Theory of Deep Convection | journal = Science | volume = 235 | issue = 4787 | pages = 465–467 | date = 1987 | pmid = 17810341|bibcode = 1987Sci...235..465C | s2cid = 21960234 }}</ref> 

==Physical intuition==
The mixing length is conceptually [[analogy|analogous]] to the concept of [[mean free path]] in [[thermodynamics]]: a [[fluid parcel]] will conserve its properties for a characteristic length, <math>\ \xi' </math>, before mixing with the surrounding fluid. Prandtl described that the mixing length,<ref name = "prandtl2">{{cite book | last = Prandtl | first = L. | title = Proc. Second Intl. Congr. Appl. Mech. | location = Zürich | date = 1926 }}</ref>
{{cquote|may be considered as the diameter of the masses of fluid moving as a whole in each individual case; or again, as the distance traversed by a mass of this type before it becomes blended in with neighbouring masses...}}

In the figure above, [[temperature]], <math>\ T</math>, is conserved for a certain distance as a parcel moves across a temperature [[gradient]]. The fluctuation in temperature that the parcel experienced throughout the process is <math>\ T'</math>. So <math>\ T' </math> can be seen as the temperature deviation from its surrounding environment after it has moved over this mixing length <math>\ \xi'</math>.

==Mathematical formulation==
To begin, we must first be able to express quantities as the sums of their slowly varying components and fluctuating components.

===Reynolds decomposition===

This process is known as [[Reynolds decomposition]]. Temperature can be expressed as:<ref name="reynolds">{{cite news|url=https://web1.eng.famu.fsu.edu/~dommelen/courses/flm/flm00/topics/turb/node2.html |title=Reynolds Decomposition | publisher=[[Florida State University]] | date=6 December 2008 | access-date=2008-12-06}}</ref>

<math display="block"> T = \overline{T} + T',</math>

where <math> \overline{T}</math>, is the slowly varying component and <math> T'</math> is the fluctuating component.

In the above picture, <math> T'</math> can be expressed in terms of the mixing length considering a fluid parcel moving in the z-direction:

<math display="block"> T' = -\xi' \frac{\partial \overline{T}}{\partial z}.</math>

The fluctuating components of velocity, <math> u'</math>, <math> v'</math>, and <math> w'</math>, can also be expressed in a similar fashion:

<math display="block"> u' = -\xi' \frac{\partial \overline{u}}{\partial z}, \qquad \ v' = -\xi' \frac{\partial \overline{v}}{\partial z}, \qquad \ w' = -\xi' \frac{\partial \overline{w}}{\partial z}.</math>

although the theoretical justification for doing so is weaker, as the [[pressure gradient force]] can significantly alter the fluctuating components. Moreover, for the case of vertical velocity, <math> w'</math> must be in a neutrally stratified fluid.

Taking the product of horizontal and vertical fluctuations gives us:

<math display="block"> \overline{u' w'} = \overline{\xi' ^2} \left | \frac{\partial \overline{w}}{\partial z}\right| \frac{\partial \overline{u}}{\partial z}.</math>

The eddy viscosity is defined from the equation above as:

<math display="block"> K_m=\overline{\xi'^2} \left| \frac{\partial \overline{w}}{\partial z}\right|,</math>

so we have the eddy viscosity, <math> K_m</math> expressed in terms of the mixing length, <math> \xi'</math>.
